tools.name: netobserv_export_flows
tools.description: Exports NetObserv flow records as CSV with the same filters as list_flows. Use when the user needs downloadable flow data for audits or offline analysis.

columns.description: Optional comma-separated column names to include (e.g. SrcK8S_Namespace,DstK8S_Namespace,Bytes). Omit to export all columns present in the result.

endTime.description: End of time range as Unix epoch seconds. Defaults to now.

filters.description:
NetObserv filter expression passed to the console plugin (plain text; the client URL-encodes it).

Syntax:
- key=value — exact match; key=a,b — OR multiple values for the same key
- key~pattern — regex / contains match; key!~pattern — NOT regex
- key!=value — not equal; key>number — numeric greater-or-equal (e.g. Bytes>1000)
- AND within a group: & (e.g. SrcK8S_Namespace=default&Proto=6)
- OR between groups: | (e.g. SrcK8S_Name=pod-a|SrcK8S_Name=pod-b)

Prefer the dedicated "namespace" parameter for namespace scope when possible.
Use Kubernetes list tools (namespaces, pods, deployments, etc.) to discover filter values.

Common Kubernetes fields (Src/Dst prefixes mirror each other):
- SrcK8S_Namespace, DstK8S_Namespace, SrcK8S_Name, DstK8S_Name
- SrcK8S_Type, DstK8S_Type (e.g. Pod, Service, Node)
- SrcK8S_OwnerName, DstK8S_OwnerName, SrcK8S_OwnerType, DstK8S_OwnerType (for Deployment, StatefulSet, etc.)
- SrcK8S_HostName, DstK8S_HostName, SrcK8S_Zone, DstK8S_Zone, K8S_ClusterName, UDN

Network & flow:
- SrcAddr, DstAddr (IPs), SrcPort, DstPort, Proto (IANA number, e.g. 6=TCP, 17=UDP)
- FlowDirection (0=Ingress, 1=Egress, 2=Inner), Bytes, Packets, Dscp, Flags

Packet drops (often with recordType flowLog and packetLoss dropped/hasDrops):
- PktDropPackets, PktDropBytes, PktDropLatestState, PktDropLatestDropCause

DNS:
- DnsName, DnsId, DnsLatencyMs, DnsErrno, DnsFlagsResponseCode

Examples:
- SrcK8S_Namespace=openshift-netobserv&SrcK8S_Name~my-app
- Proto=6&DstPort=443
- SrcK8S_Name=pod-a|SrcK8S_Name=pod-b

namespace.description: Restrict results to flows where source or destination namespace matches (dev-scoped Loki tenant).

tools.name: netobserv_get_flow_metrics
tools.description: Returns aggregated NetObserv flow metrics as topology or time-series data. Use for throughput, TLS/DNS/drop breakdowns, and namespace or workload traffic analysis; see aggregateBy and groups for grouping options.

aggregateBy.description:
Primary dimension for netobserv_get_flow_metrics (console plugin /api/flow/metrics).

Two forms (use exact spelling):

1) Topology scopes — aggregate endpoints for graph/topology views:
- app — application workloads (pods/services), excluding infrastructure traffic
- namespace — Kubernetes namespace (default)
- owner — controller owner (Deployment, StatefulSet, …)
- resource — pod, service, or node (finest workload granularity)
- host — node name
- zone — availability zone
- cluster — cluster name (multi-cluster)
- network — user-defined / secondary network name

2) Flow record fields — group by a single flow attribute (PascalCase field name).
Use for breakdown charts (TLS, DNS, drops, protocol). Field names match filters / flow logs.

TLS (requires TLS tracking on the FlowCollector):
- TLSVersion, TLSCipherSuite, TLSGroup, TLSTypes

DNS:
- DnsName, DnsFlagsResponseCode, DnsErrno

Packet drops:
- PktDropLatestState, PktDropLatestDropCause

Network / K8s (single-sided breakdown; pair with filters for src/dst):
- Proto, SrcPort, DstPort, FlowDirection, Dscp
- SrcK8S_Namespace, DstK8S_Namespace, SrcK8S_Name, DstK8S_Name
- SrcK8S_Type, DstK8S_Type, SrcK8S_OwnerName, DstK8S_OwnerName
- SrcK8S_HostName, DstK8S_HostName, SrcK8S_Zone, DstK8S_Zone
- K8S_ClusterName, SrcK8S_NetworkName, DstK8S_NetworkName

Pair aggregateBy with type and function:
- Throughput: type=Bytes or Packets, function=rate
- Flow count: type=Flows, function=count or rate
- DNS volume: type=DnsFlows, function=count
- DNS latency: type=DnsLatencyMs, function=avg, p90, or max
- RTT: type=TimeFlowRttNs, function=avg, min, or p90
- Drops: type=PktDropPackets or PktDropBytes, function=rate

Examples:
- aggregateBy=namespace, type=Bytes, function=rate
- aggregateBy=TLSVersion, type=Bytes, function=rate, filters=TLSTypes!~""
- aggregateBy=TLSGroup, type=Flows, function=count
- aggregateBy=DnsFlagsResponseCode, type=DnsFlows, function=count
- aggregateBy=PktDropLatestState, type=PktDropPackets, function=rate, packetLoss=dropped
- aggregateBy=resource, type=Bytes, function=rate, namespace=netobserv

Done.

What I changed
- Deployed canary deployment engine-v2-1 (2 replicas) in canary-deployment-ns:
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Container name: rec-engine
  - Container port: 80
  - Security configuration: same as stable (no explicit securityContext)
- Updated Service recommendation-engine to select both versions by app label only:
  - selector: app=recommendation-engine
  - Ports unchanged: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (matches current stable routing)

Result
- With engine-v2-0 at 2 replicas and engine-v2-1 at 2 replicas, the Service will send ~50% of traffic to each (distribution is proportional to the number of ready endpoints).

How to verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns rollout status deploy/engine-v2-1
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine  # should list 4 pod IPs
- Optional quick check: scale one side and observe traffic shift.

Adjusting traffic
- Change the replica ratio to alter the split (e.g., 3:1 ≈ 75/25).
- To revert to stable only, set the Service selector back to include version: v2.0 or scale canary to 0.

results.taskOutput:
I found the root cause and fixed the Deployment.

What was wrong
- The container was started with command: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, which exited immediately and caused a CrashLoopBackOff.
- Events showed BackOff restarting failed container nginx.

What I changed
- Recreated the Deployment to remove the invalid command/args so nginx runs with its default entrypoint.
- Set container image to quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged (listens on port 8080).
- Added readiness and liveness HTTP probes on / port 8080.
- Exposed containerPort 8080 and set imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent.

Current status
- Deployment crashloop-test/app is Available and Progressing = True.
- 1/1 replicas ready; Pod app-665d87db4f-k7gs8 is Running.

Anything else you’d like me to adjust (e.g., a specific command, env vars, resources, or creating a Service to expose it)?

What was wrong

outputSteps.content:
I found the root cause and fixed the Deployment.

What was wrong
- The container was started with command: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, which exited immediately and caused a CrashLoopBackOff.
- Events showed BackOff restarting failed container nginx.

What I changed
- Recreated the Deployment to remove the invalid command/args so nginx runs with its default entrypoint.
- Set container image to quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged (listens on port 8080).
- Added readiness and liveness HTTP probes on / port 8080.
- Exposed containerPort 8080 and set imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent.

Current status
- Deployment crashloop-test/app is Available and Progressing = True.
- 1/1 replicas ready; Pod app-665d87db4f-k7gs8 is Running.

Anything else you’d like me to adjust (e.g., a specific command, env vars, resources, or creating a Service to expose it)?

If you prefer to use an existing class like “standard” or “csi-hostpath-sc” instead of the new “sc”, tell me and I can switch the PVC accordingly and remove the temporary StorageClass.

Good news — it’s fixed.

- Root cause: The pod couldn’t schedule because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass “sc” (ProvisioningFailed).
- Fix applied: I created a StorageClass named “sc” using the hostpath provisioner (k8s.io/minikube-hostpath), matching your cluster’s default.
- Result:
  - PVC homepage-pvc is now Bound (1Gi, RWO).
  - Pod homepage-pod is Running and Ready.

If you prefer to use an existing class like “standard” or “csi-hostpath-sc” instead of the new “sc”, tell me and I can switch the PVC accordingly and remove the temporary StorageClass.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed two misconfigurations in your orders/webapp Deployment that kept the app from becoming Ready:

What was wrong
- Health probes: The Deployment used /is_ready and /get_status on port 80, but the nginx-unprivileged image doesn’t serve those paths and typically listens on 8080.
- Service target: The Service pointed to container port 80, which didn’t have a listener.

What I changed
- Deployment:
  - Readiness and liveness probes now hit path / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080 (left 80 present but unused; can remove if you want).
- Service:
  - targetPort updated to 8080 (port stays 80 for clients).

Current status
- Pod: webapp-5fb688dc88-4tc6s is Running and Ready (1/1).
- Deployment: Available with 1 ready replica.
- Note: You will still see earlier Warning events from the previous pod; the new pod is healthy.

How to verify
- In-cluster:
  - From any pod: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local
- From your workstation (if you want a quick check):
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward deploy/webapp 8080:8080
  - curl http://localhost:8080
- Kubernetes objects:
  - kubectl -n orders get deploy,po,svc

Optional next steps
- If you need external access, I can create an Ingress/Route for webapp on port 80 pointing to Service webapp:80 (targetPort 8080). Just say the hostname you want.

If you prefer different health endpoints or a different container image, tell me the expected paths/ports and I’ll adjust accordingly.

namespace/orders created

Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found and fixed two misconfigurations in your orders/webapp Deployment that kept the app from becoming Ready:

What was wrong
- Health probes: The Deployment used /is_ready and /get_status on port 80, but the nginx-unprivileged image doesn’t serve those paths and typically listens on 8080.
- Service target: The Service pointed to container port 80, which didn’t have a listener.

What I changed
- Deployment:
  - Readiness and liveness probes now hit path / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080 (left 80 present but unused; can remove if you want).
- Service:
  - targetPort updated to 8080 (port stays 80 for clients).

Current status
- Pod: webapp-5fb688dc88-4tc6s is Running and Ready (1/1).
- Deployment: Available with 1 ready replica.
- Note: You will still see earlier Warning events from the previous pod; the new pod is healthy.

How to verify
- In-cluster:
  - From any pod: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local
- From your workstation (if you want a quick check):
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward deploy/webapp 8080:8080
  - curl http://localhost:8080
- Kubernetes objects:
  - kubectl -n orders get deploy,po,svc

Optional next steps
- If you need external access, I can create an Ingress/Route for webapp on port 80 pointing to Service webapp:80 (targetPort 8080). Just say the hostname you want.

If you prefer different health endpoints or a different container image, tell me the expected paths/ports and I’ll adjust accordingly.

I found and fixed two misconfigurations in your orders/webapp Deployment that kept the app from becoming Ready:

What was wrong
- Health probes: The Deployment used /is_ready and /get_status on port 80, but the nginx-unprivileged image doesn’t serve those paths and typically listens on 8080.
- Service target: The Service pointed to container port 80, which didn’t have a listener.

What I changed
- Deployment:
  - Readiness and liveness probes now hit path / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080 (left 80 present but unused; can remove if you want).
- Service:
  - targetPort updated to 8080 (port stays 80 for clients).

Current status
- Pod: webapp-5fb688dc88-4tc6s is Running and Ready (1/1).
- Deployment: Available with 1 ready replica.
- Note: You will still see earlier Warning events from the previous pod; the new pod is healthy.

How to verify
- In-cluster:
  - From any pod: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local
- From your workstation (if you want a quick check):
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward deploy/webapp 8080:8080
  - curl http://localhost:8080
- Kubernetes objects:
  - kubectl -n orders get deploy,po,svc

Optional next steps
- If you need external access, I can create an Ingress/Route for webapp on port 80 pointing to Service webapp:80 (targetPort 8080). Just say the hostname you want.

If you prefer different health endpoints or a different container image, tell me the expected paths/ports and I’ll adjust accordingly.

Root cause
- The Role pod-reader-role only allowed listing deployments (apps API group) and did not grant any permission on pods (core API group), so the pod-reader service account couldn’t list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated the Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permission to list pods in the core API group.
  - Added: apiGroups: [""] resources: ["pods"] verbs: ["list"]
  - Kept existing deployments list permission intact.
- The existing RoleBinding simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-binding already targets this role and the service account simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader, so no change was needed there.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

If you also want to support kubectl get -w or fetching single pods, I can add watch/get verbs as well.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role pod-reader-role only allowed listing deployments (apps API group) and did not grant any permission on pods (core API group), so the pod-reader service account couldn’t list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated the Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permission to list pods in the core API group.
  - Added: apiGroups: [""] resources: ["pods"] verbs: ["list"]
  - Kept existing deployments list permission intact.
- The existing RoleBinding simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-binding already targets this role and the service account simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader, so no change was needed there.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

If you also want to support kubectl get -w or fetching single pods, I can add watch/get verbs as well.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so it couldn’t route traffic.
- The container listens on port 8080, but the Service targetPort was 80.
  - Even with a correct selector, traffic to port 80 would not have reached the container.

What I fixed
- Updated the Service in web/nginx:
  - Selector: app=nginx
  - targetPort: 8080 (kept Service port 80)
- Current Endpoints: 10.244.0.27:8080 (points to the running nginx pod)

Status/verification
- Deployment: 1/1 ready
- Service: ClusterIP 10.98.95.7, port 80 -> pod port 8080
- Endpoints now populated and healthy

How to test
- From inside the cluster:
  - kubectl -n web run tmp --rm -it --image=wbitt/network-multitool -- bash
  - curl -sv http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80/
- From your machine (port-forward):
  - kubectl -n web port-forward svc/nginx 8080:80
  - curl -sv http://127.0.0.1:8080/

Note on external access
- The Service is type ClusterIP, so it’s not reachable from outside the cluster unless you:
  - Change to NodePort or LoadBalancer, or
  - Expose via Ingress/Route.
- Tell me which exposure you want (NodePort/Ingress/LoadBalancer) and I can configure it.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so it couldn’t route traffic.
- The container listens on port 8080, but the Service targetPort was 80.
  - Even with a correct selector, traffic to port 80 would not have reached the container.

What I fixed
- Updated the Service in web/nginx:
  - Selector: app=nginx
  - targetPort: 8080 (kept Service port 80)
- Current Endpoints: 10.244.0.27:8080 (points to the running nginx pod)

Status/verification
- Deployment: 1/1 ready
- Service: ClusterIP 10.98.95.7, port 80 -> pod port 8080
- Endpoints now populated and healthy

How to test
- From inside the cluster:
  - kubectl -n web run tmp --rm -it --image=wbitt/network-multitool -- bash
  - curl -sv http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80/
- From your machine (port-forward):
  - kubectl -n web port-forward svc/nginx 8080:80
  - curl -sv http://127.0.0.1:8080/

Note on external access
- The Service is type ClusterIP, so it’s not reachable from outside the cluster unless you:
  - Change to NodePort or LoadBalancer, or
  - Expose via Ingress/Route.
- Tell me which exposure you want (NodePort/Ingress/LoadBalancer) and I can configure it.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so it couldn’t route traffic.
- The container listens on port 8080, but the Service targetPort was 80.
  - Even with a correct selector, traffic to port 80 would not have reached the container.

What I fixed
- Updated the Service in web/nginx:
  - Selector: app=nginx
  - targetPort: 8080 (kept Service port 80)
- Current Endpoints: 10.244.0.27:8080 (points to the running nginx pod)

Status/verification
- Deployment: 1/1 ready
- Service: ClusterIP 10.98.95.7, port 80 -> pod port 8080
- Endpoints now populated and healthy

How to test
- From inside the cluster:
  - kubectl -n web run tmp --rm -it --image=wbitt/network-multitool -- bash

Summary of findings
- Root cause: The web-app pods were Pending due to a nodeSelector constraint in the Deployment: environment=production-gpu. Your cluster’s only node doesn’t have this label, so the scheduler couldn’t place any pods. This left the Service with no endpoints, causing connection refused to web-app-service.
- Evidence:
  - Events: FailedScheduling — “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.”
  - Deployment spec had nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu.
  - Service Endpoints were empty initially.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector from the web-app-deployment so it can schedule on the available node.

Current status
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-6n2mh — Running (10.244.0.30)
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-wj2kf — Running (10.244.0.31)
- Service endpoints: web-app-service now has 10.244.0.30:80, 10.244.0.31:80
- Container is healthy (nginx started successfully).

Impact
- With pods now running and endpoints populated, traffic to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 should succeed. The frontend connection refused errors should stop.

If you intended to pin these pods to GPU/production nodes
- Either relabel the target node(s):
  - kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
- Or put the selector back with labels that actually exist on your GPU nodes.
- If you only need preferred placement, consider nodeAffinity with preferredDuringScheduling instead of a hard nodeSelector.

Recommended hardening (optional)
- Add readinessProbe and livenessProbe on port 80.
- Set resource requests/limits.
- Pin image to a specific version tag instead of latest.
- Consider a PodDisruptionBudget and a HorizontalPodAutoscaler if needed.

Would you like me to:
- Add probes and resource requests?
- Re-apply the nodeSelector with the correct node labels (or label the right nodes)?
- Run an in-cluster curl check to confirm the Service is reachable end-to-end?

namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created

deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Summary of findings
- Root cause: The web-app pods were Pending due to a nodeSelector constraint in the Deployment: environment=production-gpu. Your cluster’s only node doesn’t have this label, so the scheduler couldn’t place any pods. This left the Service with no endpoints, causing connection refused to web-app-service.
- Evidence:
  - Events: FailedScheduling — “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.”
  - Deployment spec had nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu.
  - Service Endpoints were empty initially.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector from the web-app-deployment so it can schedule on the available node.

Current status
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-6n2mh — Running (10.244.0.30)
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-wj2kf — Running (10.244.0.31)
- Service endpoints: web-app-service now has 10.244.0.30:80, 10.244.0.31:80
- Container is healthy (nginx started successfully).

Impact
- With pods now running and endpoints populated, traffic to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 should succeed. The frontend connection refused errors should stop.

If you intended to pin these pods to GPU/production nodes
- Either relabel the target node(s):
  - kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
- Or put the selector back with labels that actually exist on your GPU nodes.
- If you only need preferred placement, consider nodeAffinity with preferredDuringScheduling instead of a hard nodeSelector.

Recommended hardening (optional)
- Add readinessProbe and livenessProbe on port 80.
- Set resource requests/limits.
- Pin image to a specific version tag instead of latest.
- Consider a PodDisruptionBudget and a HorizontalPodAutoscaler if needed.

Would you like me to:
- Add probes and resource requests?
- Re-apply the nodeSelector with the correct node labels (or label the right nodes)?
- Run an in-cluster curl check to confirm the Service is reachable end-to-end?

outputSteps.content:
Summary of findings
- Root cause: The web-app pods were Pending due to a nodeSelector constraint in the Deployment: environment=production-gpu. Your cluster’s only node doesn’t have this label, so the scheduler couldn’t place any pods. This left the Service with no endpoints, causing connection refused to web-app-service.
- Evidence:
  - Events: FailedScheduling — “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.”
  - Deployment spec had nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu.
  - Service Endpoints were empty initially.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector from the web-app-deployment so it can schedule on the available node.

Current status
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-6n2mh — Running (10.244.0.30)
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-wj2kf — Running (10.244.0.31)
- Service endpoints: web-app-service now has 10.244.0.30:80, 10.244.0.31:80
- Container is healthy (nginx started successfully).

Impact
- With pods now running and endpoints populated, traffic to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 should succeed. The frontend connection refused errors should stop.

If you intended to pin these pods to GPU/production nodes
- Either relabel the target node(s):
  - kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
- Or put the selector back with labels that actually exist on your GPU nodes.
- If you only need preferred placement, consider nodeAffinity with preferredDuringScheduling instead of a hard nodeSelector.

Recommended hardening (optional)
- Add readinessProbe and livenessProbe on port 80.
- Set resource requests/limits.
- Pin image to a specific version tag instead of latest.
- Consider a PodDisruptionBudget and a HorizontalPodAutoscaler if needed.

Would you like me to:
- Add probes and resource requests?
- Re-apply the nodeSelector with the correct node labels (or label the right nodes)?
- Run an in-cluster curl check to confirm the Service is reachable end-to-end?

I’ve created the requested multi-tenant development setup in your cluster. Summary of what’s in place and how it maps to your requirements:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labels applied to enable policy scoping:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: environment=dev, role=user, owner=<name>
  - dev-shared: environment=dev, role=shared
  - staging: environment=staging, role=protected
  - prod: environment=prod, role=protected

2) RBAC
- Per-developer namespaces:
  - Role ns-full-access granting all verbs on all namespaced resources
  - RoleBinding owner-full-access binding:
    - User principals: alice in dev-alice, bob in dev-bob, charlie in dev-charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Dev-shared namespace:
  - Role read-only (get, list, watch)
  - RoleBinding devs-readonly binding users (alice, bob, charlie) and their SAs from their own namespaces
- Staging and prod:
  - No developer RoleBindings created; only cluster-admins have access by default (least privilege)
- Note: The User subject names (alice, bob, charlie) must match your identity provider usernames (e.g., OIDC, client cert CN). Adjust if needed.

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2
  - requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4
  - requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8
  - requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) Network Policies (isolation and least privilege)
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in every non-system namespace:
  - dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow DNS egress in all the above namespaces to system DNS:
  - Egress allowed to kube-system (kube-dns) and, where relevant, openshift-dns on TCP/UDP 53
- In developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - Allow same-namespace traffic (Ingress/Egress)
  - Allow to and from dev-shared only
  - No cross-developer namespace communication (blocked by default deny + explicit allows restricted to same ns and dev-shared)
- dev-shared:
  - Allow ingress from and egress to namespaces labeled environment=dev and role=user (i.e., the three developer namespaces)
- staging and prod:
  - Isolated from dev: only allow Ingress/Egress within staging/prod scopes; dev namespaces cannot reach them, and vice-versa
  - DNS egress allowed (as above)

5) Default deny policies
- Implemented in all created application namespaces (dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- Not applied to system namespaces (e.g., kube-system), in line with best practices

How to verify access and isolation
- Namespaces:
  - kubectl get ns
- RBAC checks:
  - Own namespace full access (example): kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' -n dev-alice --as alice
  - Shared namespace read-only (example):

  - kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' -n dev-alice --as system:serviceaccount:dev-alice:alice-sa
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as system:serviceaccount:dev-alice:alice-sa
  - kubectl auth can-i create pods -n dev-shared --as system:serviceaccount:dev-alice:alice-sa (should be no)
- Network isolation quick test (using a temporary netshoot pod):
  - Same namespace should succeed; cross-developer should fail; to dev-shared should succeed; to staging/prod should fail
- DNS resolution:
  - From any non-system namespace, nslookup/kdig should resolve via CoreDNS/openshift-dns

Notes and recommendations
- User identities: Ensure your auth provider issues identities exactly as “alice”, “bob”, and “charlie”, or adjust RoleBindings to match actual usernames or Groups.
- ServiceAccount tokens (Kubernetes ≥1.24): If you need a token for a developer SA, use the TokenRequest API (kubectl create token alice-sa -n dev-alice) or mount projected tokens in pods.
- System services: DNS egress is allowed. If additional “system services” are required (e.g., cluster internal registries, monitoring), add narrowly scoped egress rules to those endpoints/namespaces/ports.
- Optional hardening:
  - Add LimitRange objects with default requests/limits to complement the quotas and avoid pod admission failures or noisy neighbors.
  - If you need staging/prod to allow only specific ingress/egress between each other, further narrow those policies.

  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4
  - requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8
  - requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) Network Policies (isolation and least privilege)
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in every non-system namespace:
  - dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow DNS egress in all the above namespaces to system DNS:
  - Egress allowed to kube-system (kube-dns) and, where relevant, openshift-dns on TCP/UDP 53
- In developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - Allow same-namespace traffic (Ingress/Egress)
  - Allow to and from dev-shared only
  - No cross-developer namespace communication (blocked by default deny + explicit allows restricted to same ns and dev-shared)
- dev-shared:
  - Allow ingress from and egress to namespaces labeled environment=dev and role=user (i.e., the three developer namespaces)
- staging and prod:
  - Isolated from dev: only allow Ingress/Egress within staging/prod scopes; dev namespaces cannot reach them, and vice-versa
  - DNS egress allowed (as above)

5) Default deny policies
- Implemented in all created application namespaces (dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- Not applied to system namespaces (e.g., kube-system), in line with best practices

How to verify access and isolation
- Namespaces:
  - kubectl get ns
- RBAC checks:
  - Own namespace full access (example): kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' -n dev-alice --as alice
  - Shared namespace read-only (example):
    - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice
    - kubectl auth can-i create pods -n dev-shared --as alice  (should be no)
- ServiceAccount scope (example):
  - kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' -n dev-alice --as system:serviceaccount:dev-alice:alice-sa
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as system:serviceaccount:dev-alice:alice-sa
  - kubectl auth can-i create pods -n dev-shared --as system:serviceaccount:dev-alice:alice-sa (should be no)
- Network isolation quick test (using a temporary netshoot pod):
  - Same namespace should succeed; cross-developer should fail; to dev-shared should succeed; to staging/prod should fail
- DNS resolution:
  - From any non-system namespace, nslookup/kdig should resolve via CoreDNS/openshift-dns

Notes and recommendations
- User identities: Ensure your auth provider issues identities exactly as “alice”, “bob”, and “charlie”, or adjust RoleBindings to match actual usernames or Groups.
- ServiceAccount tokens (Kubernetes ≥1.24): If you need a token for a developer SA, use the TokenRequest API (kubectl create token alice-sa -n dev-alice) or mount projected tokens in pods.
- System services: DNS egress is allowed. If additional “system services” are required (e.g., cluster internal registries, monitoring), add narrowly scoped egress rules to those endpoints/namespaces/ports.
- Optional hardening:
  - Add LimitRange objects with default requests/limits to complement the quotas and avoid pod admission failures or noisy neighbors.
  - If you need staging/prod to allow only specific ingress/egress between each other, further narrow those policies.

If you want, I can export all applied manifests in a single bundle for version control (kustomize or a flat multi-doc YAML) or make any adjustments to labels/policies to match your environment conventions.

outputSteps.content:
I’ve created the requested multi-tenant development setup in your cluster. Summary of what’s in place and how it maps to your requirements:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labels applied to enable policy scoping:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: environment=dev, role=user, owner=<name>
  - dev-shared: environment=dev, role=shared
  - staging: environment=staging, role=protected
  - prod: environment=prod, role=protected

2) RBAC
- Per-developer namespaces:
  - Role ns-full-access granting all verbs on all namespaced resources
  - RoleBinding owner-full-access binding:
    - User principals: alice in dev-alice, bob in dev-bob, charlie in dev-charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: alice-sa in dev-alice, bob-sa in dev-bob, charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Dev-shared namespace:
  - Role read-only (get, list, watch)
  - RoleBinding devs-readonly binding users (alice, bob, charlie) and their SAs from their own namespaces
- Staging and prod:
  - No developer RoleBindings created; only cluster-admins have access by default (least privilege)
- Note: The User subject names (alice, bob, charlie) must match your identity provider usernames (e.g., OIDC, client cert CN). Adjust if needed.

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2
  - requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4
  - requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8
  - requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) Network Policies (isolation and least privilege)
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in every non-system namespace:
  - dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow DNS egress in all the above namespaces to system DNS:
  - Egress allowed to kube-system (kube-dns) and, where relevant, openshift-dns on TCP/UDP 53
- In developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - Allow same-namespace traffic (Ingress/Egress)
  - Allow to and from dev-shared only
  - No cross-developer namespace communication (blocked by default deny + explicit allows restricted to same ns and dev-shared)
- dev-shared:
  - Allow ingress from and egress to namespaces labeled environment=dev and role=user (i.e., the three developer namespaces)
- staging and prod:
  - Isolated from dev: only allow Ingress/Egress within staging/prod scopes; dev namespaces cannot reach them, and vice-versa
  - DNS egress allowed (as above)

5) Default deny policies
- Implemented in all created application namespaces (dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- Not applied to system namespaces (e.g., kube-system), in line with best practices

How to verify access and isolation
- Namespaces:
  - kubectl get ns
- RBAC checks:
  - Own namespace full access (example): kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' -n dev-alice --as alice
  - Shared namespace read-only (example):
    - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice
    - kubectl auth can-i create pods -n dev-shared --as alice  (should be no)
- ServiceAccount scope (example):
  - kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' -n dev-alice --as system:serviceaccount:dev-alice:alice-sa
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as system:serviceaccount:dev-alice:alice-sa
  - kubectl auth can-i create pods -n dev-shared --as system:serviceaccount:dev-alice:alice-sa (should be no)
- Network isolation quick test (using a temporary netshoot pod):
  - Same namespace should succeed; cross-developer should fail; to dev-shared should succeed; to staging/prod should fail
- DNS resolution:
  - From any non-system namespace, nslookup/kdig should resolve via CoreDNS/openshift-dns

Notes and recommendations
- User identities: Ensure your auth provider issues identities exactly as “alice”, “bob”, and “charlie”, or adjust RoleBindings to match actual usernames or Groups.
- ServiceAccount tokens (Kubernetes ≥1.24): If you need a token for a developer SA, use the TokenRequest API (kubectl create token alice-sa -n dev-alice) or mount projected tokens in pods.
- System services: DNS egress is allowed. If additional “system services” are required (e.g., cluster internal registries, monitoring), add narrowly scoped egress rules to those endpoints/namespaces/ports.
- Optional hardening:
  - Add LimitRange objects with default requests/limits to complement the quotas and avoid pod admission failures or noisy neighbors.
  - If you need staging/prod to allow only specific ingress/egress between each other, further narrow those policies.

If you want, I can export all applied manifests in a single bundle for version control (kustomize or a flat multi-doc YAML) or make any adjustments to labels/policies to match your environment conventions.
